takeaways: Instructions must not rely only on shape, color, size, visual location, orientation or sound to tell people what to do.
“Tap the round button on the right” means nothing to someone who cannot see the screen, or whose screen has reflowed so “right” is now “below”.
You can still mention how things look. Pair it with something that does not depend on sight or hearing: “Select Continue, the green button”.
This covers your copy as much as your layout: onboarding tips, empty states, help text and error messages. Color used alone to carry meaning is also covered by 1.4.1.
failures: “Click the icon in the top right to save”
“Required fields are in red” with no other marker
A quiz that says “Start when you hear the beep” with no visual cue
check: Search your copy for words like left, right, above, below, round, square, green, red, large and sound.
For each one, check the instruction also names the thing by its visible label or text.
Look at the instruction on the mobile layout too, where positions change.

quiz.question: An onboarding coach mark says “Tap the star to save a recipe”. The star icon has no visible label. What is the best fix?
options: Add an arrow pointing from the coach mark to the star
Make the star bigger and yellow so it stands out
Give the button a visible “Save” label and write “Tap Save (the star) to keep this recipe”
quiz.why: An arrow, a size or a color are still visual cues only. Naming the control by a text label gives everyone, including screen reader users, something to find.

spec: In every instruction, refer to controls by their visible label, and make sure that label matches the accessible name.
Where a sound signals something, specify the visual or text cue that goes with it.
Flag any copy that mentions position, so content designers keep it accurate when layouts change.
review: If you read this instruction aloud to someone over the phone, could they follow it?
Does this still make sense when the layout stacks on mobile?
Which controls here are named only by their shape or color?
tradeoff: Pointing at things by look is quick and friendly, and label-only copy can feel dry. Keep the visual hint, but always add the name: “Choose Next, at the bottom of the card”.
system: In the content guidelines, add a rule that instructions name controls by their label, and give icon-only buttons a visible or tooltip label people can refer to.
pitch: “The button on the right” is a bug the moment the layout changes. Naming things by their label works on every screen and for every user.
